explanations: terra: The commanded cow is specifically one not trained to plow or water a field, the opposite of the source section’s yaʿmala, a female camel naturally fitted for work.
terra: The pilgrim must send an available sacrificial animal and wait until it reaches its place, an earlier formulation of the camel offering’s journey and appointed slaughter.
terra: The pilgrimage passage commands taking provision while calling piety the best provision, adding the inward measure to 2:196’s animal offering and travel.

terra: The observer is told to look at his food and drink, his donkey, and the animal’s bones as God raises and clothes them; it joins commanded looking, provision, animal anatomy, and creation as evidence of resurrection.
terra: Livestock are listed among the adorned stores of worldly wealth, directly supporting the section’s Arabic picture of the camel as property and fortune.
terra: Satan’s program includes slitting livestock ears and altering God’s creation, the human mutilation of animals set against looking rightly at how the camel was created.
terra: Grazing livestock are made lawful as food while pilgrimage hunting has a limit, framing animal use as granted rather than simply possessed.
terra: Sacrificial animals and their garlands must not be violated, protecting the pilgrimage herd before the lined slaughter described in 22:36.
terra: A pilgrim who kills game owes an equivalent from livestock as an offering reaching the Kaaba, placing animal value, sacrifice, and pilgrimage under a measured legal boundary.

luna: The section cites camels lined for sacrifice at the pilgrimage. This ayah names the sacrificial offerings and garlands among the signs by which the Sacred House stands for people, placing the camel offering within the Hajj's public order. | terra: The Kaaba, sacred month, sacrificial offerings, and their garlands are made a support for people, placing the camel offering within the institutions that sustain pilgrimage life.
terra: Consecrated animal categories are rejected as human inventions; the verse checks attempts to remove valuable animals, especially camel categories, from their God-given uses.
terra: Every land animal is described as belonging to communities like humans, adding a creaturely social dimension to the camel herd beyond its value as property.
terra: People are commanded to look at fruit when it forms and ripens, another disciplined gaze at created food that can train the look directed at camel and provision.
terra: People divide crops and livestock between God and their partners, corrupting the camel herd’s status as a whole gift and form of wealth.
terra: Invented rules bar access to certain livestock backs and foods, reversing the divinely given riding and eating uses developed throughout the section.
terra: People falsely reserve what is in livestock wombs for men and exclude women, imposing a human food boundary on the animal body that God provides.
terra: Those who forbid God’s livestock provision through fabrication are declared lost, closing the false-use sequence that 6:138–139 specifies.
terra: Livestock include load-bearing animals and animals kept close to the ground, and people may eat God’s provision; this directly frames the camel as burden bearer and food.
terra: The sheep and goat pairs begin the enumeration completed by camels and cattle in 6:144, locating the camel pair within the full created livestock set rather than in isolation.

luna: The section glosses الإبل as camels and as a form of wealth. This verse explicitly names الإبل among paired livestock, then asks which sex God supposedly forbade; it places the camel herd inside a concrete argument about animal food and its limits. | terra: The camel pair is named explicitly while false claims about males, females, and womb contents are challenged, adding sex and reproduction to the image of the created camel body.

terra: The verse details a restriction on cattle and sheep fat, except what clings to backs, entrails, or bones; it directly illuminates the section’s س م ن branch, marrow fat, and edible animal body through a legal boundary.

luna: The section places the camel as an ordinary creature close to human life just after describing a garden. This ayah says the deniers will not enter the Garden until a camel passes through a needle's eye, using the same animal to mark an impossible boundary to entry. | terra: A camel cannot pass through a needle’s eye, and that bodily scale marks the barred entry to heaven; the animal invited as a visible sign in the section becomes a measure of impossibility.

luna: The section asks the reader to look at the created camel and notes its relation to pasture. In this account, the she-camel is God's sign and is left to eat on God's earth; the animal's grazing becomes a test of how people treat a provision. | terra: Salih presents God’s she-camel as a sign, tells his people to let her graze in God’s land, and forbids harm; camel, pasture, creation-sign, and human responsibility all meet.

terra: Immediately after the she-camel warning, Thamud are reminded of palaces on the plain and homes carved in mountains; their fixed architecture illuminates by contrast the camel-skin dwelling carried through a journey.
terra: The people hamstring the she-camel and defy their Lord’s command, reversing 7:73’s required gaze, grazing freedom, and care into destruction.

terra: The hypocrites would have followed for near gain and an easy journey, but the distance seemed too great; that failed journey clarifies why the camel’s ability to carry people far is a consequential provision.
terra: Thirst, fatigue نَصَب, and hunger incurred on a journey in God’s path form the same bodily triad as the section’s water-saving, feeding, day-traveling camel.
terra: Rain-fed growth eaten by people and livestock suddenly becomes reaped debris, showing the transience of the pasture on which the camel’s sufficiency depends.

luna: The section links the camel to grazing and sustenance. This account also commands the people to leave God's she-camel to eat from God's earth, then warns them not to harm her; it presents animal provision as something humans must respect. | terra: The she-camel is God’s sign and must be left to feed in His land, directly repeating the camel-at-pasture scene and its protected status.
terra: After the she-camel is hamstrung, only three days remain before punishment; the killed sign turns the useful protected animal into the boundary of judgment.
terra: Abraham brings a roasted calf to his guests, another livestock body turned into generous food beside the section’s marrow, fat, and meat senses.
terra: A caravan sends its water-drawer and a bucket brings Joseph up, pairing desert travel with the act of drawing water that also governs the camel’s life.

luna: The section names س م ن as the root behind ghee from milk and notes that 88:7's food does not fatten. This ayah's dream of seven fat cows consumed by seven lean cows makes animal fatness a measure of abundant and failing provision. | terra: Seven lean cows consume seven fat cows, using animal fatness as the visible boundary between abundance and famine beside the section’s fat, food, and livestock wealth.
terra: Joseph is asked about seven fat cows consumed by seven lean ones, repeating the animal-fat image of 12:43 while explicitly seeking its meaning for the coming abundance and famine.
terra: The brothers expect an added camel-load of grain, so the camel’s carrying capacity becomes a unit of measured provision and family subsistence.
terra: A drinking cup is placed in a saddlebag before the caravan is hailed; cup, baggage, provisioning, and camel travel meet just as milk cups and journey meet in the section.

luna: The section brings camel milk together with cups and the camel as a carrier. In Yusuf's story, the missing royal cup is paired with a reward of a camel's load; the ayah joins vessel and caravan measure in a distinct scene. | terra: The lost drinking cup is paired with a camel-load as reward, again joining vessel, load, value, and caravan economy in one ayah.

luna: The section explicitly links its word for milk that goes down easily, سَائِغًا in 16:66, with the swallowing root in this ayah. The condemned person gulps the boiling drink but can hardly swallow it, reversing the section's image of drink made easy for the recipient. | terra: The hell-dweller gulps the drink ولا يكاد يسيغه, the exact reversal of the livestock milk that is سَائِغًا in 16:66 and of the section’s nourishing camel drink.
terra: No fatigue touches the people of the garden and they will not be expelled, opposing the tiring movement and temporary night stop contained in the section’s camel vocabulary.

luna: The section's lexical note connects نَاعِمَة to نَعَم, livestock, and to blessing. This verse names al-anʿām as created for warmth, benefits, and food, grounding that wordplay in the practical good the animals provide. | terra: God creates livestock for warmth, benefits, and food, directly presenting the camel as a created, many-sided human provision.

luna: The section's journey lexicon describes a full day of travel followed by camping at night. This verse pictures livestock being brought home in the evening and sent out in the morning, giving that daily rhythm a concrete herd scene. | terra: Livestock are beautiful when brought home in the evening and driven to pasture in the morning; that daily herd rhythm makes concrete the section’s day-long camel travel and return at night.

luna: The section sets the nearby camel against far sky, mountains, and earth, and develops the animal as a carrier. This verse says livestock carry loads to a distant land people could not reach without great strain, making the camel's everyday closeness tangible. | terra: Livestock carry human loads to a country people could scarcely reach unaided, directly matching the camel as mount, bearer, and means of distant travel.

luna: The section treats the camel as a mount and carrier. This neighboring livestock passage names horses, mules, and donkeys for riding and adornment, placing the camel's transport role among other created mounts. | terra: Horses, mules, and donkeys are named for riding and adornment after the load-bearing livestock, defining the camel’s place among other mounts by comparison.

luna: The section describes a camel that can subsist on moist growth without first drinking. This verse sends down water for people to drink and says vegetation grows where livestock graze, linking water, pasture, and the animal's nourishment. | terra: Water descends for human drink and grows vegetation in which animals graze, directly joining the section’s water, fresh pasture, and camel subsistence.

luna: The section's root note for تُسْقَى (س ق ي) includes a waterskin for water and milk. Here God gives people pure, easy-to-swallow milk from between waste and blood, showing the camel's milk-and-waterskin vocabulary against a startling account of animal provision. | terra: Pure, easy-swallowed milk is given from inside livestock between waste and blood; it directly realizes the section’s udder, milk, watering, and ساغ detail.

luna: The section says the camel helps furnish the room. This verse names animal hides for houses and their wool, camel hair, and other hair for furnishings and use, making the dwelling's animal materials explicit. | terra: Livestock skins become portable houses and their wool, fur, and hair become furnishings and goods, exactly the section’s claim that the camel furnishes the room around its rider.
terra: Human beings are carried on land and sea and given good provisions; the land half is realized concretely by the burden-bearing mounts paired with ships elsewhere.

luna: The section's root note for نَاصِبَة includes a group's whole-day walk. In this ayah Moses' companion says the journey has caused fatigue, a concrete travel use of the same root named for the section's laboring faces. | terra: Moses’ companion says that their journey has brought fatigue نَصَبًا, the direct travel sense activated by the section’s ن ص ب dictionary branch.
terra: Moses beats down leaves with his staff for his sheep, a concrete herdsman action that parallels managing a camel herd’s access to forage.

luna: The section's camel is sustained by pasture. This verse says rain brings forth varied plants and directs people to eat and let their livestock graze, directly naming the animal's food. | terra: God makes paths through the earth and sends water that produces paired plants, joining the camel journey’s route to the pasture eaten in 20:54.
terra: People are told to eat and pasture their livestock among the plants God brings forth, directly staging shared human and animal provision.
terra: Sheep graze through a cultivated field by night, showing that pasturing a herd also requires custody and boundaries, not merely available vegetation.

luna: The section reads the root of 88:1's “came” as a camel's forelegs moving in a walk. Here lean camels bring pilgrims from every distant pass; the dictionary gait becomes an actual caravan arrival. | terra: Lean mounts come from every deep pass to the pilgrimage; their يأتين joins the source section’s gait sense under أ ت ي with the camel’s long-distance journey.

luna: After the section cites the camel sacrifice in 22:36, this neighboring Hajj verse says to eat from the livestock offering and feed the distressed poor. It supplies the distribution of sacrificial food in its own passage. | terra: Pilgrims mention God over sacrificial livestock, eat from them, and feed the destitute, anticipating the lined camel and feeding instructions of 22:36.
terra: Honoring God’s ritual symbols is traced to the piety of hearts; this supplies the inward stance for the sacrificial animals called divine symbols in 22:36.

luna: The section presents the camel as useful wealth and names rows of sacrificial camels. This Hajj verse says the sacrificial animals benefit people for a set term before their destination is the Ancient House, joining practical use to the offering's endpoint. | terra: Sacrificial animals provide benefits until their appointed term and destination at the Ancient House, joining useful livestock with pilgrimage and eventual slaughter.
terra: Every community receives a rite in which God’s name is mentioned over the livestock He provides, setting the broader rule behind the section’s sacrificial camels.

luna: The section's lexical note identifies مَصْفُوفَة as rows of sacrificial camels; this ayah has camels standing صَوَافَّ as God's name is recalled, then directs eating and feeding the content and the asker. Ordered camels, remembrance, and provision meet in one rite. | terra: Sacrificial camels stand صَوَافَّ in rows, God’s name is spoken over them, then their meat feeds both the contented القانع and the asker; this gathers the section’s camel, صفّ, remembrance, sufficiency, food, and subjection in one scene.

luna: The section pairs sacrifice with naming God and feeding people in 22:36. This neighboring ayah says neither the animals' flesh nor blood reaches God, but piety does; it clarifies what the feeding and sacrifice signify. | terra: Neither the animals’ meat nor blood reaches God; piety does, and their subjection should produce magnification and gratitude, defining the spiritual boundary of the camel sacrifice in 22:36.

luna: The section follows camel milk from udder to cup. This ayah calls livestock a lesson, says people are given drink from their bellies, and names their other benefits and meat; it makes milk one part of the animal's broad provision. | terra: Livestock provide milk from their bellies, many other benefits, and food, concentrating the same animal body and human uses traced through the section.

luna: After 23:21 names milk and the livestock's benefits, this neighboring verse says people are carried on animals and ships. It supplies the transport side of the camel's usefulness in the section. | terra: People are carried on livestock and ships; after 23:21’s milk and food, this adds the camel’s transport function.
terra: God creates every animal from water and includes those walking on four legs; the camel belongs to that created class even though the section stresses its unusual ability to delay drinking.
terra: People who neither hear nor reason are likened to livestock and judged further astray, a pointed reversal of the section’s expectation that a human should look at the camel and learn from it.

luna: The section follows the camel's relation to water and grazing. This verse describes rain sent to revive dead land and to provide drink for livestock and many people, joining animal thirst to renewed pasture. | terra: Rain revives dead land and gives drink to many livestock and people, linking divine watering to the herd’s life rather than treating water as an isolated substance.
terra: Livestock and children are named as reinforcements of worldly abundance, confirming the herd as a visible form of wealth and divine provision.
terra: Gardens and springs form part of Thamud’s secure abundance in the speech that soon introduces the she-camel, supplying the water-rich setting against which her allotted drink matters.
terra: Crops and laden palms add pasture and food abundance to the same Thamud setting before the she-camel’s water share is imposed.
terra: Thamud carve skillful houses from mountains in the she-camel passage; these fixed stone dwellings contrast with the portable houses the section says livestock skins provide.

luna: The section's camel is an animal whose water needs are unusual and whose milk is carried. This account assigns God's she-camel a set day to drink and the people their own day, making access to water the exact point of the sign. | terra: The she-camel receives an allotted turn to drink and the people theirs, a precise boundary around س ق ي that counters the section’s camel able to subsist on moist pasture.

luna: After the camel's water turn is specified in 26:155, this verse warns the people not to touch her with harm. It reverses the section's attentive regard for the camel into a scene where people violate the sign. | terra: Salih forbids touching the she-camel with harm and ties violation to a tremendous day, stating the moral boundary around 26:155’s shared water.
terra: They hamstring the she-camel and become regretful, the direct reversal of allowing the animal its measured drink.
terra: At Midian shepherds water their flocks while two women hold theirs back, staging herd, herder, and scarce shared water around the same س ق ي relation as the camel passages.
terra: Moses waters the women’s animals, supplying the act withheld in 28:23 and turning access to water into care for a herd.
terra: People are commanded to travel through the earth and observe how God began creation, uniting the camel’s function as a means of travel with the section’s command to look at how it was created.

luna: The section says the camel can be satisfied by fresh growth. This verse describes water reaching barren land and crops that people and their livestock eat, setting out the provision on which grazing depends. | terra: People are asked whether they see water driven to barren land and crops eaten by both their livestock and themselves, closely matching the section’s look at camel and food.

terra: Mountains are commanded to echo or return with David under the أ و ب root; the source section uses that root for the camel’s day journey and evening return, so even the distant mountain participates in responsive return.
terra: No morally burdened soul can make another carry its load, whereas the camel mercifully carries loads people could not transport themselves; literal service marks the limit of moral transfer.
terra: Livestock vary in color alongside people and other creatures, supplying another visible feature through which an observer can recognize deliberate animal creation.

luna: The section's root note for نَاصِبَة describes a group's day-long walk, beside the exhausted labor of 88:3. This ayah says no fatigue or weariness touches the people in the enduring home, reversing toil with settled ease. | terra: The lasting abode is a place where no fatigue نَصَب touches its people, the restful endpoint that answers the source section’s all-day journey and 18:62’s travel weariness.

luna: The section names 88:3's عَامِلَة as a root with a branch describing a working camel. Here the root occurs in “what Our hands have worked” to describe God's creation of livestock for people; work shifts from the exhausted faces to the Creator's making. | terra: God asks whether people see that His hands’ work, عملت أيدينا, created livestock for them; this directly answers the section’s working-camel sense of ع م ل by relocating the decisive work to God.

luna: The section presents the camel as a familiar useful creature. This verse says the animals were made serviceable for people, who ride some and eat some, directly spelling out two of the camel's ordinary benefits. | terra: God makes the livestock tractable, ذللناها, so people ride and eat; the same lowering that can mark humiliation becomes mercy when applied to the camel.

luna: The section tracks milk and its delivery in vessels. This continuation says the livestock provide other benefits and drinks, extending the camel's bodily provision beyond food and riding. | terra: Livestock give further benefits and drinks, completing 36:71–72’s creation, riding, and eating with the section’s milk-bearing animal.

luna: The section develops lined-up sacrificial camels and cushions, using the root ص ف ف for an ordered row. This ayah swears by those ranged in rows; whatever the rowed beings are, it gives a parallel of deliberate alignment.
luna: The section explains that the cups in paradise can hold milk. This ayah depicts cups passed among the blessed from a flowing spring, a close parallel between the promised cup and its source.
luna: The section describes cups set out in a garden with a flowing spring. This verse calls the drink white and delightful to drinkers, giving the promised beverage its pleasant quality.
terra: Zaqqum is a tree growing in the root of Hell, a fire-grown plant that reverses the source dictionary’s ordinary fodder plant called “camel bread.”
terra: The condemned eat from Zaqqum and fill their bellies, a punitive plant meal opposed to the little fresh forage that suffices the camel.

terra: The “great sacrifice” that ransoms Abraham’s son plausibly belongs beside the camel offerings of 22:33–37 as another divinely provided sacrificial animal, though this ayah itself does not name its species.
terra: The birds are gathered and each is أَوَّاب, turning the source section’s return-at-night root into a collected creaturely return rather than a camel caravan.
terra: One ewe versus ninety-nine makes herd size a form of property and power, a smaller-animal parallel to the camel wealth named in the section.
terra: The eight livestock pairs and their formation in wombs place sex, gestation, and animal creation behind the section’s milk-bearing female camel.

luna: The section's camel is a humanly near asset, and its dictionary discussion includes riding. This verse says God made livestock so people can ride some and eat some, stating the paired use directly. | terra: God makes livestock so that people may ride some and eat some, a direct summary of the camel’s two central uses in the section.

luna: The section describes the camel as a carrier and source of benefit. This verse names further benefits, carrying needs on livestock and ships, so it broadens the camel's role from food and riding to transport. | terra: Livestock meet needs held in human breasts and carry people as ships do, extending 40:79 from food and riding to purposeful travel.

luna: The section's dictionary note for خ ش ع describes a camel's hump losing fat and drooping. This ayah calls the dry earth خَاشِعَة, then says rain makes it stir and grow; the root's lowered state turns toward the fresh growth that sustains grazing animals. | terra: The humbled earth خَاشِعَةً stirs and swells after rain; the source section’s خ ش ع branch describes an exhausted camel hump sinking, while this use leads back to the rain-fed pasture that restores animal life.
terra: God makes livestock in pairs and multiplies them, giving the reproductive basis of the herds treated as wealth and milk-bearing provision in the section.

luna: The section develops the camel as a mount. This verse says God made livestock and ships as mounts, directly placing animal travel beside sea travel. | terra: God creates the pairs and provides ships and livestock as mounts, locating camel travel within the ordered gift of creation.

luna: The section's camel is both a creature to observe and a blessing people use. This verse says riders should settle on the animals' backs and remember their Lord's favor, connecting the mount to gratitude. | terra: The rider settles on the mount’s back and remembers the One who subjected it; this is the section’s striking relation that the camel is beside the human while the human is upon it.
terra: The mount prayer ends by declaring return to the Lord, joining the section’s camel journey and nightly return to the surah’s final return to God.
luna: The section pictures a garden furnished with cups. This ayah has golden platters and cups carried around among the blessed, a direct parallel in the arrangement of garden vessels.
terra: The tree of Zaqqum begins another Qur’anic hell-food scene, a fire-grown counterpart to the source dictionary’s ordinary fodder plant called “camel bread.”
terra: Zaqqum is identified as the sinner’s food, turning a plant into punishment rather than the small amount of herbage that sustains the camel.
terra: Human creation and the animals God disperses are signs for people of certainty, directly generalizing the invited gaze at the camel as a created sign.

terra: Disbelievers eat as livestock eat before the Fire becomes their dwelling; this reverses the section’s modestly sufficient camel by showing humans consuming without understanding or saving themselves.

luna: The section's garden has a running spring and placed cups, while its other scene has an un-swallowable drink in Hell. This description contrasts the two destinations through rivers of fresh water and milk, and boiling water for the Fire's people. | terra: Paradise contains rivers of milk whose taste never changes, extending the section’s pure animal milk and prepared cups into an unspoiled heavenly provision.
terra: Sacrificial animals are detained from reaching their appointed place at Hudaybiyya, a historical interruption of the pilgrimage movement and slaughter completed in 22:33–36.

luna: The section's camel is shown beside the far sky, mountains, and earth as a sign to look at. This ayah also asks people to look at the sky above and how it was built, extending the same gaze from nearby creature to distant creation.

luna: The section sets the camel's familiar body against mountains and the spread earth. This verse names the spread earth and firmly placed mountains, closely paralleling the surrounding landscape of its gaze.

luna: The section moves from looking at created signs to the command to remind. This ayah says the sky and earth scene is insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back, linking observation to remembrance.
terra: Abraham brings his guests a fat calf; the livestock’s fatness, under the section’s س م ن branch, becomes food and hospitality.

luna: The section develops مَصْفُوفَة as rows of cushions and, in its lexical note, rows of sacrificial camels. This ayah describes the blessed reclining on couches مَصْفُوفَة, carrying the same ordered furnishing into the garden scene.

luna: The section places cups among the garden's furnishings and says no idle speech is heard there. This ayah depicts the blessed passing a cup among themselves with neither idle speech nor sin, joining the cup scene to the garden's quiet.

luna: The section names the root س ع ي for the striving of the garden's satisfied faces. This ayah says a person has only what they strove for, making the link between earthly effort and the section's contentment in the afterlife explicit. | terra: A human has only what he strives for, giving moral consequence to س ع ي while the source section’s dictionary branch uses the root for a moderate physical run within the camel journey.

luna: The section names سَعْي as effort and says the garden's faces are satisfied with it. This ayah says that effort will be seen, adding the disclosure of the work whose outcome the section describes.
luna: The section's faces are pleased with their striving. This continuation says each person will then be repaid with the fullest recompense, supplying the outcome of the striving named in 53:39–40.

luna: The section treats the camel itself as a sign to be observed. This ayah calls the she-camel a trial and commands the audience to watch, giving the animal a testing role as well as a created one. | terra: God sends the she-camel as a trial and commands watchful patience, making the animal itself a divine sign at which humans must learn how to look.

luna: The section develops the camel's relation to water and drinking. This verse says the water is apportioned among the people and the she-camel, making the animal's drink a matter of shared measure. | terra: Water is divided and every drinking turn attended, supplying the concrete watering rule for the she-camel introduced in 54:27.
terra: The people summon their companion, who seizes and hamstrings the she-camel, turning the watched trial of 54:27 into deliberate violence.
terra: God raises the sky and sets down the balance, placing the section’s ر ف ع and و ض ع opposition in a cosmic ordering rather than an animal gait.

luna: The section describes a garden furnished with raised couches and arranged cushions. This ayah pictures the blessed reclining on couches whose linings are brocade, a specific continuation of the garden's furnishings.

terra: The Event is “lowering, raising,” a judgment-day pairing that echoes the source section’s opposed raised and lowered camel gaits while distinguishing those side senses from the ayah’s cosmic reversal.

luna: The section explains its garden cups through the image of vessels being filled from a camel's milk. This ayah's garden has cups, pitchers, and a cup from a flowing spring, making the vessel-and-drink scene explicit. | terra: Paradise attendants carry goblets, pitchers, and a cup from a flowing spring, extending the section’s meeting between a milk-giving camel, cups filled in sequence, and the furnished Garden.

luna: The section's lexical note for the root ر ف ع calls a she-camel that holds colostrum in her udder a rāfiʿ, while 88:13 has raised couches. This ayah repeats the raised-couch garden scene, making the root's shift from bodily holding to elevated furnishings concrete.

luna: The section sets an animal that can be satisfied by little fresh growth against people whose food fails them. This ayah assigns the people of the left the fruit of the Zaqqūm tree, an afterlife food scene on the opposite side of that contrast. | terra: The wrongdoers eat from the tree of Zaqqum; this hell plant is a dark counterpart to the source dictionary’s pasture plant called “camel bread” and begins the scene ending with thirsty camels in 56:55.

luna: The section contrasts an animal's modest grazing with people left unsatisfied in 88:6–7. This verse says the condemned fill their bellies from the Zaqqūm, making the quantity of food no remedy for the torment. | terra: They fill their bellies from Zaqqum, turning a plant into compulsory excess rather than the camel’s modest sufficiency; 56:55 supplies the camel comparison.

luna: The section contrasts the easy drink of milk with the afterlife's harsh drink. This verse says the people of the Fire drink boiling water after their food, giving the scene of thirst its own punishing beverage. | terra: Boiling water follows the hell food, joining eating and forced drinking before 56:55 likens the drinkers to thirsty camels.

luna: The section's camel can subsist on fresh growth without needing to drink first. Here the people of the Fire drink like thirsty camels, reversing that image into desperate, unrelieved thirst. | terra: The condemned drink like desperately thirsty camels, reversing the section’s camel that can make do with moist pasture and completing 56:52–54’s hell food-and-drink scene.
terra: The community had urged neither horses nor riding camels toward the recovered property, so the exact camel mount appears through the absence of a journey or charge.
terra: A mountain would become humbled and split from fear of God; it transfers the source section’s خ ش ع image of a collapsed camel hump to the distant high object set beside the camel in surah 88.
terra: A donkey bearing books provides a negative image of animal load-bearing: physical carriage remains while human understanding fails, unlike the camel’s load as an intelligible blessing.
terra: God makes the earth tractable, tells people to walk its paths and eat His provision, and ends with resurrection to Him; it parallels the tractable camel’s route, food, and ultimate return.

luna: The section describes people in Hell with no food except a plant that neither fattens nor relieves hunger. This ayah likewise says there is no food for the condemned but ghislin, a direct parallel in the deprivation of the afterlife meal.
terra: Mountains become like wool on the last day, bringing the distant mountain together with the animal fiber that the section says supplies furnishings and portable homes.
luna: The section's cups belong to the garden's provision. This ayah says the righteous drink a cup mixed with camphor, giving a specific drink to set beside the section's offered cups.
luna: The section joins cups to a flowing spring. This verse says the righteous drink from a spring that God's servants make flow, supplying the source behind a garden cup.
luna: The section's cup imagery includes vessels arranged in the garden. This ayah describes silver vessels and cups passed around, furnishing a direct parallel for placed cups.
luna: The section describes a cup as a vessel for milk. This ayah names a cup mixed with ginger in the garden, giving another concrete drink carried by a cup.
luna: The section's garden includes a running spring beside its cups. This ayah identifies a spring named Salsabil, completing the drink's source in its own scene.
terra: Huge sparks are thrown from the fire; this ayah supplies the object whose shape or movement 77:33 compares with yellow camels.

luna: The section sets a camel in view alongside the hot Fire scene. This ayah likens the Fire's sparks to yellow camels, making the animal itself the scale and shape of a fiery image. | terra: Hell’s sparks are likened to yellow camels, bringing the section’s familiar animal into the fire scene that precedes its command to look.

luna: The section places the camel beneath a sky described as raised. This neighboring creation passage says the sky's ceiling was raised and proportioned, echoing the sky that frames the camel in 88:17–20.

luna: The section's creation gaze ends with the spread earth around the camel. This ayah says the earth was spread out, echoing that ground in the same sequence that continues with water, pasture, and mountains.

luna: The section's camel lexicon describes an animal sustained by fresh growth rather than water. This verse says God brought water and pasture from the earth, naming the two parts of that provision together. | terra: From the spread earth God brings out its water and pasture, the two resources whose unusual relation defines the camel in the section.

luna: The section places the camel in a landscape of distant mountains. This neighboring ayah says God set the mountains firmly in place, extending the same creation scene around the camel and pasture.

luna: The section treats the camel as a creature kept by provision and made useful to people. This verse calls what came before provision for people and their livestock, giving grazing animals a place in the creation scene. | terra: Water, pasture, and the ordered earth are declared provision for people and livestock, completing 79:31 in the same human-animal pairing as 80:32.

luna: The section asks the reader to look at the camel as a nearby created sign. This ayah likewise commands a look, directing attention to human food; it makes eating itself an object of reflection. | terra: The command that the human look at his food repeats the section’s commanded gaze at the camel while redirecting sight toward the provision the animal also supplies.
terra: Poured water is the first material step in the food chain opened at 80:24 and completed as provision for livestock at 80:32.
terra: The earth is split open so growth can emerge, preparing the pasture and animal provision named later in 80:31–32.
terra: Grain is one product of the opened earth in the inspected food scene whose conclusion includes livestock.
terra: Grapes and green fodder are brought forth; the vegetation gives concrete content to the camel’s fresh-herbage diet before 80:32 names livestock.
terra: Olives and palms add human food to the same created provision that culminates in shared human and livestock benefit.
terra: Dense gardens locate the growing environment from which 80:31’s fruit and pasture emerge for the two beneficiaries of 80:32.

luna: The section's camel can live on fresh growth. This ayah names fruit and herbage among the earth's produce, bringing grazing growth into the food sequence. | terra: Fruit and pasture are the last named growth in the food sequence; the pasture specifically prepares 80:32’s provision for livestock and the camel that lives from fresh herbage.

luna: The section develops the camel as an animal sustained by what grows and useful to people. This ayah calls the preceding food a provision for people and their livestock, explicitly joining human and animal sustenance. | terra: The whole food scene is declared a provision for people and their livestock, explicitly completing the gaze begun at 80:24 with the human-animal pair developed in the section.

luna: The section treats the camel as familiar wealth and a source of everyday provision before the final return to God. This ayah says pregnant she-camels are abandoned amid the Last-Day upheaval; a normally valuable herd is neglected when judgment arrives. | terra: At the final upheaval even pregnant she-camels, prized living wealth, are abandoned; this sharply confirms the section’s camel-as-fortune while showing fortune’s limit.

luna: The section's root note describes camels and wild animals getting by on fresh growth. This verse says God brought out the pasture, naming the plant world at the center of that lexical image. | terra: God brings out fresh pasture, the very food by which the source section says the camel can dispense with direct water for a time.
terra: Fresh pasture becomes dark stubble, setting the camel’s moist sustaining herbage against the same vegetation after it has lost its nourishment.

luna: The section asks readers to regard the camel and recalls its dependence on pasture rather than frequent water. This ayah names God's she-camel and its turn to drink, foregrounding the animal's access to water. | terra: God’s messenger warns the people to respect God’s she-camel and her drink, again binding the camel sign to a protected share of water.

luna: The section's camel is a creature to be contemplated and provisioned. This ayah says the people hamstrung God's she-camel, turning regard for the animal into its violent opposite. | terra: They deny the messenger and hamstring the she-camel, so destruction follows; the creature whose drink was protected in 91:13 becomes the test they fail.
terra: God removes the Prophet’s burden, using the source section’s و ض ع root in a figurative unloading that 94:3 locates on the back.
terra: The burden had weighed upon the back, making 94:2’s relief a pointed human counterpart to the camel carrying another’s heavy load.
terra: Panting mounts charge at speed, a sharp gait contrast to the source section’s gentle all-day camel walk and its lexicon of faster and slower steps.
terra: Mountains become like fluffed wool, a repeated judgment-day reversal in which the fixed object set opposite the camel takes on the appearance of livestock fiber.
terra: Quraysh’s winter and summer caravan journeys provide the social and economic setting in which camel travel, nightly stopping, and animal wealth belong together.
terra: The command وانحر plausibly evokes animal sacrifice, traditionally including the camel slaughter enacted explicitly in 22:36, though this ayah itself does not name the animal.
